questions.q: What is the key difference between application-level logs and what auditd captures?
options: Application logs show only what the app was coded to log; auditd logs kernel-level syscalls and file access per configured rules, regardless of whether any app mentioned them
auditd only works on web servers, never on other applications
Application logs and auditd capture exactly the same information
auditd replaces /var/log entirely and application logs no longer exist
questions.explain: auditd works at the kernel layer, watching syscalls and file access directly based on rules, so it catches activity even when an application never logs it itself.

questions.q: In `auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k shadow_changes`, what does the `-p wa` flag specify?
options: Watch for write and attribute-change access to the path
The priority level of the audit rule
The user allowed to read the watched file
A wildcard that watches all files, not just /etc/shadow
questions.explain: -p sets the permission types to watch for — w (write) and a (attribute change) here — while -k tags matching events with a searchable label.

questions.q: Why would a rule added directly with auditctl need to also be written into /etc/audit/rules.d/?
options: Rules entered with auditctl at runtime are not persistent and vanish on reboot, while rules in /etc/audit/rules.d/ are loaded automatically via augenrules
auditctl rules only apply to one user session
/etc/audit/rules.d/ is required for any rule to take effect at all, even temporarily
There is no difference — both methods are permanent by default
questions.explain: A rule set with auditctl directly disappears at reboot. For a rule that needs to survive a restart, it has to be written into a file under /etc/audit/rules.d/.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between ausearch and aureport?
options: ausearch filters the audit log for specific matching events; aureport produces a summarized report across a category like authentication or file access
ausearch and aureport are two names for the exact same command
aureport can only be run by root, while ausearch can be run by any user
ausearch summarizes events while aureport shows full raw detail
questions.explain: ausearch is for pulling specific matching events (by key, file, user, or time), while aureport gives a faster, summarized overview of a category before drilling in further.

questions.q: In the lesson's /etc/shadow example, why does ausearch still show the change even though the text editor used to make it never logs anything about /etc/shadow specifically?
options: The persistent audit watch rule logs the write/attribute event at the kernel level regardless of what the editor itself was coded to log
Text editors are hard-coded to always report changes to /etc/shadow
ausearch scans the filesystem directly instead of reading audit.log
The change was actually logged by the passwd command, not by auditd
questions.explain: Because the watch rule operates at the kernel syscall level, any process that writes to or changes attributes on /etc/shadow triggers a logged event, independent of that process's own logging behavior.
